es.heading: 11 de diciembre: el aniversario de un paso hacia la autonomía canadiense
es.origin: Cada 11 de diciembre, Canadá recuerda el Estatuto de Westminster, ley británica promulgada el 11 de diciembre de 1931. El texto siguió a las Conferencias Imperiales de 1926 y 1930 y reconoció la autonomía legislativa de los dominios autónomos, incluido Canadá. fr.heading: 11 décembre : anniversaire d'une étape de l'autonomie canadienne

Ce texte faisait suite aux conférences impériales de 1926 et de 1930 et reconnaissait l'autonomie législative des dominions autonomes, dont le Canada. Selon Patrimoine canadien, les bâtiments fédéraux disposant de deux mâts peuvent arborer l'Union Jack aux côtés du drapeau national du Canada, qui conserve la préséance. en.heading: 19 April: Korea's 1960 democratic uprising becomes an official remembrance day
en.origin: The Republic of Korea's April 19 Revolution Day recalls the student-led and citizen protests of 19 April 1960 against fraudulent elections and authoritarian rule. South Korea's Ministry of the Interior traces a separate commemorative process: the authorities recommended student ceremonies on 19 April 1962, then formally established a statutory commemoration under the national commemorative-days regulation on 30 March 1973. en.heading: 5 April: Korea's Arbor Day shifts from public holiday to civic campaign
en.origin: South Korea's Arbor Day on 5 April is linked to a longer history of national tree-planting initiatives. The Korean Ministry of the Interior notes that a 1910 tree-planting ceremony under the Korean Empire preceded the modern observance; during Japanese rule, a different Arbor Day date, 3 April, was also used. A presidential decree on 4 June 1949 made 5 April a statutory public holiday. The day was temporarily changed in 1960 and restored to 5 April in 1961, then included as a statutory commemoration in 1982. From June 2005 the date ceased to be a general public holiday while remaining a commemorative day. These shifts show why the modern date and civic status cannot be described as unchanged since 1910.

en.heading: 16 October: Busan and Masan democratic protests receive a national day
en.origin: The Bu-Ma Democratic Protests began on 16 October 1979, with demonstrations by Pusan National University students against authoritarian rule. By 18 October the protests had spread to Masan and Changwon. These decisions reflected recognition of the historical struggle for democracy but did not originate that movement. A first actual ceremony under the 2019 national statute is not established in the institutional chronology and is left unknown.

en.heading: Third Monday in May: Korea's coming-of-age tradition becomes a modern public day
en.origin: South Korea's Coming of Age Day celebrates the responsibilities and civic standing of people entering adulthood. The Ministry of the Interior traces the much older Korean coming-of-age tradition to historical court records, including a Goryeo ceremony in 965. The modern statutory commemorative day was designated on 30 March 1973, originally falling on 20 April. The government changed it to 6 May in 1975 and to the third Monday in May in September 1984, establishing today's movable schedule. These shifts explain why the date is not a fixed traditional birthday or an unchanged medieval anniversary. The 1973 statutory recognition is distinct from earlier family and court coming-of-age ceremonies. No independently verified inaugural modern government ceremony is claimed.

en.heading: 5 May: Korean Children's Day predates the current statutory holiday
en.origin: Children's Day in Korea originated in the early twentieth-century children's rights movement led by Bang Jeong-hwan and youth groups. A primary 1923 newspaper source, preserved by the Korean History Institute, calls for recognition and respect for children, documenting the first commemorative activities around 1 May 1923. en.heading: 8 October: Peru commemorates Miguel Grau and the naval battle of Angamos
en.origin: Peru remembers the naval Battle of Angamos, fought on 8 October 1879 during the War of the Pacific, when Admiral Miguel Grau was killed aboard the monitor Huáscar. The date also became part of the national Navy Day tradition. The Peruvian Congress' historical legal account identifies Law 9126 of 3 June 1940, which formally declared 8 October a national tribute to Grau and his companions and dedicated it to the flag oath of naval cadets. It followed an earlier 1921 law that already tied Navy Day to the naval battle, while further changes to Navy Day's own calendar followed in 1945. The 1940 tribute and the 1879 battle are distinct; the first actual ceremony under the 1940 commemorative act is not independently documented in the original sources, and remains unknown.

Una ricostruzione legale del Congresso peruviano cita la legge 9126 del 3 giugno 1940, che designò l'8 ottobre come giorno di omaggio nazionale a Grau e ai suoi compagni e lo collegò al giuramento alla bandiera dei cadetti navali. Esisteva già una legge del 1921 che univa la Giornata della Marina alla battaglia, mentre altri cambiamenti del calendario navale seguirono nel 1945. L'omaggio del 1940 è un fatto distinto dallo scontro del 1879; la prima cerimonia svolta sotto quella specifica norma non è documentata indipendentemente e resta sconosciuta.

en.heading: 7 June: Peru distinguishes the Battle of Arica and modern Flag Day law

en.heading: 22 September: UNESCO recognizes the living heritage of nomadic communities
en.origin: On 6 November 2025 UNESCO's 43rd General Conference, meeting in Samarkand, adopted the proclamation of 22 September as International Day of Nomadic Heritage under agenda document 43 C/51. Kyrgyzstan initiated the proposal, with Kazakhstan among its co-sponsors, as confirmed by governmental accounts of the conference. Kazakhstan's foreign ministry explains that 22 September was associated with the autumn equinox, symbolizing harmony between people and nature. The day seeks greater recognition of pastoralist knowledge, seasonal migration, traditional crafts and intergenerational teaching, without implying nomadic ways of life began with UNESCO's declaration. Separate UNESCO intangible-heritage decisions have already recognized practices such as Mongol nomad migration. The proclamation followed September 2025, and no first annual observance in September 2026 is individually evidenced by the consulted original documents; the inaugural-year field remains unknown.

La proposta fu avviata dal Kirghizistan e sostenuta fra gli altri dal Kazakistan, secondo i resoconti governativi della conferenza. en.heading: 9 April: the Philippines remembers Bataan with a statutory Day of Valor
en.origin: The Philippines' Republic Act No. 3022, approved on 6 April 1961, proclaimed 9 April Bataan Day and established it as a legal holiday in memory of the soldiers and civilians who defended the Bataan Peninsula during the Second World War. The date recalls the surrender of forces on Bataan on 9 April 1942, preceding the brutal Bataan Death March. Article 1 of the 1961 statute explicitly asks people to observe one minute of silence at 4:30 in the afternoon. In 1987 President Corazon Aquino's Executive Order 203 listed the date among regular holidays under the name Araw ng Kagitingan, or Day of Valor, commemorating Bataan and Corregidor. The 1961 founding law, 1942 military event and 1987 name are distinct; the source does not independently prove the first official public ceremony after adoption.

en.heading: 12 October: Italy creates a modern Christopher Columbus observance in 2004
en.origin: An Italian Prime Minister's Directive dated 20 February 2004 designated 12 October every year as National Christopher Columbus Day. The directive was proposed by the Minister for Italians Abroad, Mirko Tremaglia, and signed by Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi. It instructed public administrations to support initiatives about the historical voyage that reached the Americas on 12 October 1492. The act also created an honorary committee to coordinate activities, and the Italian Presidency's records show that President Carlo Azeglio Ciampi received the committee on 5 October 2004, when the official logo was presented. The historical landfall in 1492, the 2004 formal decree and that October preparatory event are separate; the latter does not independently prove the first full annual ceremony on 12 October. The voyage is an appropriate topic for considering both transatlantic contacts and the grave consequences of European colonization for Indigenous peoples.

en.heading: Second Monday in October: Columbus Day becomes a United States federal holiday
en.origin: The United States Congress first adopted a joint resolution on 30 April 1934 requesting annual presidential Columbus Day proclamations, reflecting older community celebrations associated with Italian-American heritage. The federal holiday itself was created in the Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 and took effect in 1971, placing the observance on the second Monday of October rather than always 12 October, the date associated with Columbus's 1492 landfall in the Caribbean. The National Archives distinguishes the 1934 proclamation requirement from the 1968 federal holiday law and its actual start in 1971. Archived White House proclamations show presidents continuing the annual ceremony under 36 U.S.C. 107. The historical legacy is contested: the voyage also opened an era of European conquest, forced displacement and violence against Indigenous peoples. That complex history should be part of educational context without falsely suggesting Congress had enacted a federal holiday in 1934.
en.promoter: The US Congress established the federal public holiday through the Uniform Monday Holiday Act in 1968; an earlier 1934 congressional resolution requested presidential proclamations.
en.purpose: Examine the historical legacy of transatlantic contact and its continuing interpretations, including Italian-American heritage and the effects on Indigenous societies.

it.heading: Secondo lunedì di ottobre: negli USA il Columbus Day diventa festa federale

Il giorno festivo federale vero e proprio fu invece introdotto dall'Uniform Monday Holiday Act del 1968, entrato in vigore nel 1971: per questo la festa cade il secondo lunedì di ottobre e non sempre il 12 ottobre, data tradizionalmente collegata allo sbarco di Colombo nei Caraibi nel 1492. Gli Archivi nazionali distinguono la richiesta di proclamazioni del 1934 dalla legge federale del 1968 e dall'applicazione del 1971. I proclami presidenziali conservati nell'archivio della Casa Bianca mostrano la continuità delle celebrazioni. La storia è oggetto di discussione perché il viaggio aprì anche una fase di conquista europea, spostamenti forzati e violenze contro i popoli indigeni. Questo contesto non va ignorato né confuso con l'istituzione della festa.

en.heading: 24 April: Canada's parliamentary recognition of Armenian genocide remembrance
en.origin: On 24 April 2015 the Canadian House of Commons adopted Motion M-587, moved by MP Brad Butt. It reaffirmed the House's earlier Armenian-genocide recognition resolution of 21 April 2004, recognized April as Genocide Remembrance, Condemnation and Prevention Month and expressly identified 24 April as Armenian Genocide Memorial Day. The date recalls the arrests of Armenian intellectuals in Constantinople on 24 April 1915, explained in a contemporary statement by the Armenian ambassador in Ottawa. en.heading: 28 September: Canada remembers the British Home Children
en.origin: On 7 February 2018 the Canadian House of Commons approved Motion M-133, moved by MP Guy Lauzon, urging national recognition of British Home Child Day each 28 September. The motion honours over 100,000 children brought to Canada from Britain through child-migration programmes; many were separated from their families and placed in agricultural or domestic labour. The national parliamentary acknowledgment followed a provincial statute: Ontario's British Home Child Day Act received Royal Assent on 1 June 2011 and designated the same September date. The two legal milestones must not be conflated: Ontario enacted a binding provincial law, whereas M-133 expressed the federal House's view rather than legislating a new national public holiday. The original specific reason for selecting 28 September and the first nationally organized ceremony are not demonstrated in these two measures.

Il riconoscimento federale seguì una legge provinciale: il British Home Child Day Act dell'Ontario ricevette l'assenso reale il 1º giugno 2011 e stabilì la stessa data. I due atti hanno diversa natura: quello dell'Ontario è una legge, mentre la mozione esprime l'indirizzo della Camera e non crea una festività federale non lavorativa. en.heading: First Sunday in June: Canada's day to thank its armed forces
en.origin: On 31 May 2002 Canada's prime minister proclaimed the first Sunday in June as Canadian Forces Day, responding to a unanimously supported private member's motion. The 2005 Department of National Defence announcement explicitly called that year's 5 June celebration the fourth annual Canadian Forces Day: this contemporaneous sequence independently confirms the inaugural year of 2002. Later public statements use the name Canadian Armed Forces Day. The annual commemoration recognizes regular and reserve personnel, their families and service at home and abroad, including disaster response, peace operations and humanitarian support. Because its recurrence is the first Sunday of June, the numbered date changes each year. It is a public recognition day rather than a fixed calendar anniversary or a substitute for Remembrance Day.

en.purpose: Recognize the service of Canadian Armed Forces members and their families and increase public awareness of their work.

it.heading: Prima domenica di giugno: il Canada ringrazia le proprie Forze armate
it.origin: Il 31 maggio 2002 il primo ministro canadese proclamò la prima domenica di giugno Canadian Forces Day, accogliendo una mozione parlamentare d'iniziativa individuale approvata all'unanimità. Un comunicato del Ministero della difesa del 2005 definì la celebrazione del 5 giugno di quell'anno la quarta edizione annuale: la sequenza contemporanea conferma quindi il debutto nel 2002. In seguito si è diffuso il nome Canadian Armed Forces Day. La giornata riconosce il contributo del personale in servizio e di riserva, delle famiglie e delle missioni in Canada e all'estero, compresi soccorsi, operazioni di pace e aiuti umanitari. Poiché cade la prima domenica di giugno, il giorno del mese varia ogni anno. È una ricorrenza pubblica distinta dal Remembrance Day e non un anniversario numerico fisso.

La jornada reconoce a militares en activo y reservistas, a sus familias y las tareas realizadas dentro y fuera del país: rescate, ayuda ante desastres, operaciones de paz y asistencia humanitaria. La fecha cambia cada año; no es un aniversario fijo ni sustituye al Día del Recuerdo.

L'appellation Journée des Forces armées canadiennes a ensuite gagné du terrain. Cette journée rend hommage aux militaires réguliers et réservistes, à leurs proches et à leurs missions au Canada comme à l'étranger : secours, interventions lors de catastrophes, maintien de la paix et aide humanitaire. en.heading: 6 October: Slovak Dukla remembrance changes name but retains its wartime date
en.origin: Slovakia's National Council adopted Act No. 241/1993 on 20 October 1993 and included 6 October among national memorial days under the original name Day of the Victims of Dukla. On 24 November 2015 lawmakers adopted Act No. 409/2015, effective 1 January 2016, which renamed the existing date Day of the Heroes of the Carpathian-Dukla Operation. The historical reference is the crossing of the Czechoslovak border by advance elements of the First Czechoslovak Army Corps at Dukla Pass on 6 October 1944 during the fight against Nazi Germany. The military operation itself began on 8 September 1944 and continued until late October. The National Memory Institute documents the campaign and its losses. The event of 1944, first memorial-day law of 1993, and change of official title in 2015/2016 must not be confused; an individually evidenced inaugural 1993 or 1994 memorial ceremony remains unknown.
en.promoter: Slovakia's National Council formally recognized the October memorial through Act 241/1993 and renamed it in Act 409/2015.
en.purpose: Remember people who fought and died during the Dukla operation while strengthening careful public historical understanding of World War II.

Il 24 novembre 2015 il Parlamento adottò la legge n. 409/2015, efficace dal 1º gennaio 2016, che rinominò la stessa data Giorno degli eroi dell'operazione dei Carpazi-Dukla. L'episodio ricordato è il passaggio del confine cecoslovacco da parte delle avanguardie del Primo corpo d'armata cecoslovacco al passo di Dukla il 6 ottobre 1944, nella guerra contro la Germania nazista. L'operazione militare era iniziata l'8 settembre e proseguì fino a fine ottobre. L'Istituto slovacco per la memoria nazionale documenta la campagna e le perdite umane. Evento del 1944, prima legge commemorativa del 1993 e cambio di nome del 2015/2016 sono tappe distinte; non è provata una precisa cerimonia inaugurale dopo la legge.

en.heading: 27 October: Slovakia remembers the Černová shooting of 1907
en.origin: The original Slovak Act 241/1993, adopted by the National Council on 20 October 1993, designated 27 October a national memorial day for the Černová tragedy. The date refers to 27 October 1907 in Černová, now a district of Ružomberok, when gendarmes of the Kingdom of Hungary shot into a crowd protesting the planned consecration of a new church without local-born priest Andrej Hlinka. Hlinka had been suspended, and villagers demanded the event be delayed. Fifteen people died and others were injured. In 2007, Slovakia's parliament marked the centenary, describing fifteen deaths, twelve serious injuries and subsequent prosecutions of residents. These events became central to Slovak historical memory and contemporary discussion of minority rights and government repression. The shooting in 1907, statutory memorial designation in 1993 and centenary resolution in 2007 are separate milestones; the first annual state ceremony under the 1993 law cannot be established from these documents.
en.promoter: The National Council of the Slovak Republic established the commemorative date in Act 241/1993; its subject is the villagers affected by the 1907 shooting.
en.purpose: Remember people killed in Černová and encourage historical study of civil rights, community identity and the consequences of repression.

it.heading: 27 ottobre: la Slovacchia ricorda la tragedia di Černová

La data richiama il 27 ottobre 1907, quando a Černová, oggi parte di Ružomberok, i gendarmi del Regno d'Ungheria spararono contro una folla che protestava per la prevista consacrazione di una nuova chiesa senza il sacerdote locale Andrej Hlinka. Hlinka era stato sospeso e gli abitanti chiedevano di rinviare la cerimonia. Morirono quindici persone e altre furono ferite. Nel 2007 il Parlamento slovacco commemorò il centenario, ricordando quindici morti, dodici feriti gravi e successivi processi contro i residenti. L'episodio entrò nella memoria storica nazionale e nel dibattito sui diritti delle minoranze e sulla repressione. Sparatoria del 1907, riconoscimento legislativo del 1993 e risoluzione del centenario del 2007 sono passaggi distinti; la prima cerimonia annuale sotto la legge non è provata.
